                          Purpose and Main Components of a Thesis

      Topic 1: Purpose of the Thesis                                       (MID Term paper pattren)

      To enable students to develop:                                       no mcqs
         •   deeper knowledge                                              6 Questions of 5 marks
         •   understanding
         •   capabilities                                                  Must attempt 4 questions out of 6

mcq   Overall goal is for student to display knowledge and capacity to:

         •   contribute to research and development work
         •   deal with complex theoretical issues
         •   to plan and use adequate methods and evaluate

      Thesis at the end of the programme offers the opportunity to:

         •   delve deeply into
         •   and synthesize acquired knowledge

   •   Audience and Purpose
          - Context of writing
          - Range of audience
          - Authority readers or ‘critics’

   mcq -    Scholarly community
        -   Real and imagined

   •   Secondary Audience
         -   External examiners
         -   Representative of scholarly community

Topic 3: Order and Component of Thesis (L.Q)

   1. Title page
   2. Statement of originality/ copyright page
   3. a) Dedication
       b) Acknowledgements
   4. Abstract
   5. Table of Contents
   6. List of :
       - Tables
       - Figures/ illustrations
   7. List of Abbreviations
   8. Chapters
       • Introduction
       • Literature Review
       • Methodology
       • Results
       • Discussion
       • Conclusion
   9. References
   10. Appendices

Title should SUMMARIZE the main idea:

   •   be concise
   •   highlight key variables
   •   full explanatory

   Topic 7: Footnotes and Endnotes

      •   Footnotes
             o Appear at the bottom of the page
             o Separated from the text
             o Single-spaced
             o Double-spaced line between each note

             o Additional information

             o Be inserted with the use of computer software-numbering options

thesis where the main findings, interpretations, and implications of the research are

summarized. It ties together the various threads of the argument and provides a sense
of closure to the reader.

Generative writing refers to a technique where the focus is on generating ideas and
content without being overly concerned with editing or correctness. It encourages
free-flowing creativity and exploration of ideas, which can be particularly useful
during the initial stages of writing to overcome writer's block or to explore different
angles of a topic.

minimum number of words necessary to convey the intended meaning. It avoids
unnecessary repetition, wordiness, and ambiguity, making the text more readable
and effective in communicating the author's message.

written form. In academic contexts, writing involves researching, drafting, revising,

understanding within a particular field.

permission, or ability. Examples include "can," "could," "may," "might," "must,"

used to convey degrees of certainty, obligation, or speculative interpretation.

headings.

charts, diagrams, photographs, or illustrations that are used to present data or
enhance understanding of concepts. Types of figures can include line graphs, bar

charts, scatter plots, and more complex diagrams depending on the nature of the data
being presented.

sentences or those under ten are often written out in words for clarity and style
consistency.

EDU705
Thesis Purpose

The overarching aim of a thesis, which is to demonstrate the student's ability to contribute to
research, solve theoretical issues, and apply appropriate methods.

Thesis Components

The sections or parts of a thesis, including title page, abstract, introduction, literature review,
methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, and appendices.

Writing Style

The tone, structure, and formatting choices made to ensure clarity, coherence, and appropriateness
for the academic audience.

Primary Audience

The immediate readers of the thesis, such as the academic community, supervisors, or examiners.

Secondary Audience

People outside the primary audience, such as policymakers or general readers interested in the
findings.

Title Page

The first page of a thesis that includes the title, author’s name, and institution.

Abstract

A concise summary of the thesis, presenting its aims, methodology, findings, and significance.

Table of Contents

An outline listing chapters, sections, and their corresponding page numbers.

Statement of Originality

A declaration that the work presented is the author’s original work and has not been plagiarized.

Acknowledgements

A section where the author expresses gratitude to individuals or institutions that contributed to the
research.

Footnotes

Notes placed at the bottom of a page, providing additional information or citations related to the
main text.

Endnotes

Similar to footnotes but located at the end of a chapter or thesis, often used to reduce page clutter.

Introduction Chapter

The opening section of a thesis that introduces the research problem, significance, and the overall
structure of the thesis.

Literature Review

A comprehensive analysis of existing research, identifying gaps and establishing the context for
the current study.

Research Gap

A specific area or question in a field that has not been sufficiently explored and forms the basis of
the study.

Niche

The unique position or contribution of the research within the broader field of study.

Signposting

Writing techniques that guide the reader through the structure and flow of the thesis.

Dedication

An optional section where the author honors someone by dedicating the thesis to them.

Hierarchy in Thesis

The structure or levels of headings, sections, and subsections within the thesis.

Appendices

Supplementary materials that support the thesis, such as data tables, transcripts, or ethical
approvals.

Research Territory

The broader context or field of study that the research addresses, highlighting its relevance and
scope.

Aims of Study

Clear, concise statements about what the research intends to achieve.

Key Constructs

The main concepts or variables used in the research, which are often socially or theoretically
defined.

Background Research

Previous studies and theories that provide context for the current research.

Problem Statement

A precise articulation of the research issue that needs to be addressed.

Gap Identification

Highlighting areas in existing literature where knowledge is lacking.

Occupying a Gap

Explaining how the research addresses the identified gap through its aims, methodology, and
contribution.

Linguistic Features

The language choices made in academic writing, such as tense, voice, and style, to convey meaning
effectively.

Present Perfect Tense

Used to discuss research conducted in the past but relevant to the present study.

Simple Present Tense

Used for established facts, generalizations, or current state of knowledge.

Simple Past Tense

Used to describe specific completed actions or past methodologies.

Paraphrasing

Rewriting ideas from a source in your own words while preserving the original meaning and
properly citing it.

Coherence

Ensuring ideas are logically connected and flow smoothly throughout the thesis.

Synthesizing

Integrating multiple sources and perspectives to create a cohesive argument or summary.

Reporting Verbs

Verbs used to discuss or critique others' work, such as "argued," "claimed," or "proposed," which
reflect the author’s stance.

Plagiarism

The unethical act of presenting someone else's work or ideas as one’s own without proper
acknowledgment.

Methodology

The section describing the research design, methods, and rationale behind choosing those methods.

Ethical Concerns

Considerations related to privacy, consent, and fair treatment of research participants.

Validity

The degree to which a research method measures what it claims to measure.

Reliability

The consistency and accuracy of a research method or instrument over time.

Data Collection

The process of gathering information using tools such as surveys, interviews, or observations.

Data Analysis

The methods used to interpret and make sense of the collected data.

Sampling

Selecting participants or data points for research based on specific criteria.

Triangulation

Using multiple methods, data sources, or theories to increase the reliability and validity of the
findings.

Research Paradigm

The underlying framework or philosophy guiding the research, such as qualitative, quantitative, or
mixed-method approaches.

Qualitative Data

Non-numerical data, such as interviews or observations, focusing on themes and meanings.

Quantitative Data

Numerical data, such as statistics or survey responses, focusing on measurable variables.

Findings

The results or outcomes of the research, presented as evidence supporting the research question.

Discussion Chapter

A section that interprets findings, relates them to existing research, and discusses their
implications.

Conclusion Chapter

The final section that summarizes findings, highlights contributions, and provides
recommendations or future research directions.

The methodology of a research study outlines the procedures and techniques used to collect,
analyze, and interpret data. It typically includes the research design (qualitative, quantitative, or
mixed methods), sampling methods (random, stratified, convenience), data collection tools
(surveys, interviews, experiments), and data analysis techniques (statistical analysis, thematic
analysis, content analysis). The methodology ensures the research is systematic, valid, and reliable,

Q. Feature of abstract
A key feature of an abstract is its conciseness, offering a succinct summary of the main points of
a larger work such as a research paper, thesis, or report. It typically includes the purpose of the

The abstract allows readers to quickly ascertain the paper's relevance and significance, providing
a snapshot that helps them decide whether to read the full document. It should be clear, precise,
and free of unnecessary details, ensuring that even those unfamiliar with the full text can
understand the essence of the work.

Q. What is the choice of tense in the citing statement?
The choice of tense in citing statements depends on the context of the reference. Present tense is
used when discussing the current relevance or established facts from a study, such as "Smith (2020)
argues that social media influences consumer behavior." Past tense is appropriate for referring to
specific experiments or studies conducted in the past, for example, "Johnson (2018) found that
increased exercise improves mental health." Present perfect tense is used to discuss past research
with ongoing relevance, like "Researchers have shown that climate change affects biodiversity
(Green et al., 2015)." Selecting the appropriate tense helps clarify the relationship between past
research and its current implications.

Q. Where is 'Hedging' used in the reporting results? Explain.
Hedging is used in reporting results, particularly in academic and scientific contexts, to convey
uncertainty, caution, and modesty about findings. It allows authors to acknowledge limitations,
avoid overstatements, and respect the scientific process by using language that softens or qualifies
statements. Phrases like "may," "might," "could," "suggests," and "is likely to" help present
findings accurately, indicating that results are not absolute or universally applicable. For example,
"The results suggest a potential link between diet and heart health" is more accurate than making
a definitive claim. Hedging ensures claims are appropriately cautious, inviting critical discussion
and further inquiry.

Glossary
                         A special Thanks to “Minha”
   Correlation
Interdependence between factors within a system.
   Deductive reasoning
An approach to research where the researcher predicts a relationship between the
independent and dependent variables, stating it as a hypothesis. The hypothesis is
then tested to see if it is true or false. Comes under the logic of reasoning.
   Dependent Variable
The outcome variable. In experimental research, this variable is expected to depend
on a predictor (or independent) variable.
   Research Question
A clear statement in the form of a question of the specific issue that a researcher
wishes to analyze.
   Sampling

The process of selecting a subgroup of a population that will be used to represent the
entire population.
   Semi-Structured Interview
A method of data collection in which the interviewer uses a pre-determined list of
topics or questions to gather information from a respondent. The interviewer,
however, may stray from the list to follow-up on things the respondent says during
the interview.

               Notes for Mids
      Purpose of the Thesis: it serves as a formal document where you present
      original research or scholarly work on a specific topic. It demonstrates your
      understanding, critical thinking, and ability to contribute new knowledge
      Writing Style and Audience:
         - Writing style refers to how you express ideas, use language, and
            structure sentences.
         - Consider your audience (readers) when choosing a style. Academic
            writing is typically formal, precise, and objective.
      Order and Component of Thesis
         - Title page: Includes title, author, institution, and date.
         - Abstract: Brief summary of the thesis.
         - Table of Contents: Lists chapters and sections.
         - Introduction: Sets context and outlines research question.
         - Literature Review: Surveys existing research.
         - Methodology: Describes research methods.
         - Results: Presents findings.
         - Discussion: Analyzes results.
         - Conclusion: Summarizes key points.
         - References: Lists cited sources.
         - Appendices: Additional material (e.g., data, charts).
         - Acknowledgments: Thanks to supporters.
         - Statement of Originality: Affirms original work.

Footnotes and Endnotes: footnotes appear at the bottom of pages, while
endnotes are at the end of chapters or the entire document. They provide
additional information or references.
Abstract: it summarizes your thesis briefly. It helps readers decide if they
want to read the full document.
Key Linguistic Feature of an Abstract: Tense: Abstracts often use the
present tense to discuss general truths or current relevance
Questions Related to Abstract Writing
   - "How long should the abstract be?"
   - "What should I include?"
   - "How do I make it engaging?"
Introduction Chapter in a Thesis: it sets the stage for your research. It
outlines the problem, research question, and significance.
Functions of the Introduction Chapter
   - Engagement: It captures the reader's attention and sets the tone for the
       entire work.
   - Context: It provides background information related to the topic.
   - Thesis Statement: It clearly defines the research problem or question.
   - Significance: It explains why the study is relevant and valuable.
   - Structure: It outlines the organization of the thesis or research paper.
Introduction: Establishing a Research Territory: In this section, you
demonstrate knowledge of the topic and its relevance to the field. You explain
where your study fits within existing literature and establish the context for
your research.
Indicating a Gap/ Niche: You highlight a gap or limitation in previous
research. By identifying this gap, you emphasize the need for further
investigation in your specific area.
Occupy the Niche/ Gap: This step involves presenting new information or
results that address the identified gap. You contribute to the field by filling
the gap with your research findings.
Statement of the Problem and the Context: The statement of the problem
defines the research issue or question. The context provides background
information related to the problem.

Aims of the Study: The aims outline the specific goals or objectives of your
research. They guide your investigation and provide direction.
Clarification of Key Constructs: You define essential terms, concepts, or
variables used in your study. This ensures clarity and understanding for the
reader.
Organization of the Thesis: You briefly describe how the thesis or research
paper is structured. This helps readers navigate through your work.
Key Linguistic Features in Establishing Significance of the Study: These
include language cues that emphasize the importance of your research. For
example, phrases like "critical gap" or "novel contribution" signal
significance.
Key Linguistic Features in Indicating the Gap: These features highlight
limitations or areas lacking sufficient research. Contrastive phrases (e.g.,
"however," "despite") often signal this.
Key Linguistic Features in Occupying the Gap in the Introduction: Here,
you present specific results or findings that address the gap. Use clear
language without interpretation or evaluation.
Active vs. Passive Voice Use
   - Active voice emphasizes the doer of the action (e.g., "We conducted
       the study").
   - Passive voice focuses on the action itself (e.g., "The study was
       conducted").
Key Linguistic Features: Adjectives and Pronouns
   - Adjectives add precision (e.g., "significant," "promising").
   - Pronouns (e.g., "we," "our") personalize the research.
Language Use in Making Comparisons: Comparative language (e.g.,
"compared to," "in contrast") highlights differences. Use it to discuss existing
research or your own findings
Introduction: Questions Answered: The introduction should address the
"what" and "why" of your research. It sets the stage for the reader to
understand your study

Footnotes and Endnotes: Understanding the Differences
Both footnotes and endnotes serve the purpose of providing additional information
within a written document, but they differ in their placement and function. Here's a
breakdown:
Placement:
   • Footnotes: These appear at the bottom of the page where the reference is made
     in the main text. A superscript number in the text (like this¹²) corresponds to a
     matching numbered footnote at the bottom of the page.
   •  Endnotes: These are listed at the end of the entire document, typically after the
      main text and before the bibliography. A superscript number in the text links to a
      corresponding numbered entry in the endnote section.
Function and Length:
  • Footnotes: Generally used for brief explanations, comments, or additional
       details that might distract the reader from the main flow of the text. They are ideal
       for short citations or minor points.

          o   Example 1 (Footnote): "The population of Earth is estimated to be around
              8 billion people.¹" (Footnote at bottom of page): ¹ Source: Worldometer
          o Example 2 (Footnote): "Shakespeare's birthplace, Stratford-upon-Avon, is
            a popular tourist destination for fans of the Bard.²" (Footnote at bottom of
            page): ² Source: Shakespeare's Birthplace Trust
   •   Endnotes: Can be used for longer explanations, quotations, or even
       bibliographic references (depending on the style guide). They are better suited
       for in-depth information that wouldn't disrupt the reading experience.
           o Example 1 (Endnote): "A recent study by the National Institute of Health
               suggests a link between green tea consumption and improved cognitive
               function."(Endnote section): ¹ National Institute of Health. (2023). Green
              tea and cognitive health: A review of the latest research.
          o   Example 2 (Endnote): "As the Supreme Court Justice stated in a landmark
              decision, 'Justice delayed is justice denied.'"(Endnote section): ² This
              quote is attributed to William Blackstone, but the specific source needs to
              be identified for proper citation.
Choosing Between Footnotes and Endnotes:
  • Use footnotes for brief remarks or minor citations that would break the flow of the
     text if included elsewhere.
  • Use endnotes for longer explanations, extensive references, or information that
      wouldn't be essential for immediate understanding.
Additional points to consider:
  • Some style guides (like Chicago) allow for using either footnotes or endnotes,
      while others (like APA and MLA) have specific guidelines for referencing sources
       within the main text.
   •   Footnotes can sometimes clutter the page, while endnotes can disrupt the
       reading flow if the reader needs to flip back and forth frequently.
